title: A map of the world in squares
teaches: Tile pyramids, how many tiles each zoom needs, pre-rendering against rendering on demand, vector tiles, and versioned map updates

blocks.text: On 8 February 2005 Google opened Google Maps. Online maps already existed; on MapQuest, the most used, you clicked an arrow at the edge of the map and the whole page went away and came back with a new picture shifted half a screen over. On Google's you took hold of the map and dragged it, and it slid under the pointer, with new country appearing at the edges as fast as you could pull. It came from Where 2 Technologies, a small company founded in Sydney by the brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen with Noel Gordon and Stephen Ma, which Google had bought the October before.[^ajax]

The trick was that the map was not one picture. The world had been cut, at every zoom level, into square images 256 pixels on a side, called **tiles**, and the page asked the server for whichever tiles were in view, plus a border of them just outside it. As you dragged, JavaScript fetched the next squares in the background and placed them beside the ones already there. Each tile was an ordinary image file at an ordinary address, so every browser cache and every cache between the browser and Google could keep a copy.

That design raises the questions this lesson answers. How many squares does the whole world need, down to the zoom where you can see the lanes on a road? Which of them should be drawn ahead of time, and which only when someone first looks? And when a road opens, how do you change the map that a billion cached squares already show? This lesson opens the Maps and places branch, lessons M1 to M4, which follow the systems behind an online map: its tiles, the nearest car, routes and live traffic. OpenStreetMap, the open map Steve Coast started in London in 2004, faces the same questions in public, and where its answers are public they are noted below.

First the world must become a square. Web maps use the **Web Mercator** projection, which draws the globe on a cylinder, unrolls it, and cuts it off at about 85° north and south, where the stretched polar regions would make it taller than wide.[^mercator] At **zoom** 0 the whole square is one tile. At each zoom after that, every tile is cut into four, so zoom *z* is 2^*z* tiles across and 2^*z* down, 4^*z* in all. A tile is named by three numbers, its zoom and its column and row: 14/2624/5722 is the zoom-14 tile with downtown Seattle in it, and the tile's address on the server is built from those three numbers.

First the numbers. At zoom 0 the 40,075 km of the equator are spread over 256 pixels, about 157 km a pixel. Each zoom halves that. Zoom 10 is about 150 metres a pixel, a town. Zoom 18 is about 60 cm, enough to see the lanes of a road.

blocks.caption: The tiles at each zoom. The square on the left shows the grid up to zoom 6 and the tile that holds Seattle; the bars count the tiles at each zoom, each line on the scale ten times the one below it.
blocks.task: Guess, then go down to zoom 18

blocks.text: Zoom 18 alone has 4^18, about 69 billion tiles, and every zoom from 0 to 18 together about 92 billion, a third more than the deepest level, since each level holds a quarter as many tiles as the next deeper one. At 20 KB a tile, a fair size for a compressed map image, drawing all of them would take nearly two petabytes, before the zooms beyond 18 that phones now use. That is the first wrong design: drawing every tile at every zoom in advance.

parts.title: What to draw ahead of time

blocks.text: Most of those tiles are never looked at. About 71% of the Earth's surface is sea, and a deep-zoom tile of open ocean is a plain blue square. A tile store can keep one copy of that square and point every ocean address at it. Of the land, most is desert, ice, forest and farmland that hardly anyone zooms into. Requests pile up instead on cities and roads, and on the zooms people use to find a street or a neighbourhood, so popularity is as skewed as it was for the films in lesson 19's edge caches: a small share of the tiles gets most of the requests.

So the usual design splits the pyramid. The low zooms are few and everyone sees them, so they are drawn ahead of time and kept. The deep zooms are drawn the first time someone asks for one, in about 50 milliseconds of computing for a land tile, then stored and cached like the rest. OpenStreetMap's tile servers work this way: a tile not yet drawn is drawn on request, together with its neighbours in a block of eight by eight, since drawing one block costs little more than drawing one tile.[^metatile]

blocks.caption: Where to draw the line between tiles drawn ahead and tiles drawn on demand. The mix of requests across zooms is a made-up but typical shape; the storage and drawing time follow from the tile counts at 20 KB and 50 ms a land tile.
blocks.task: Move the line down to zoom 18 and read the cost

blocks.text: With the line at zoom 12 there are 22 million tiles, of which about 6.7 million have land on them. At 20 KB for each land tile and one shared copy of the blue square for the rest, that is about 130 GB, and it can be drawn in minutes on a thousand cores, and they serve about a quarter of all requests. Each zoom further down multiplies the cost by four and adds a smaller share of the requests. The tiles drawn on demand cost the first viewer a wait, but only the first, because lesson 19's caches hold every tile after that: the browser's own cache, then the edge of a content delivery network near the reader, then the tile store. A screen of 1,920 by 1,080 pixels shows about forty tiles, and a few dozen more load for a drag, so a busy map serves hundreds of thousands of tiles a second, nearly all of them from caches.

Maps change every day: a road opens, a shop closes, a name is corrected. The change shows on one tile at each zoom where it is visible, perhaps two or four if it sits near a tile's edge, so a single edit dirties about one tile per zoom. Finding them is geometry: take the edit's bounding box, widen it by the largest line width or label drawn around it, and list the tiles it overlaps at each zoom. A new version redraws only those tiles and points every other address at the previous version's copy, so it costs about as much as its changes. Low zooms change constantly because each one covers so much, so their tiles are drawn again in batches, the kind of job lesson 8's MapReduce was built for.

The harder part is the caches. A tile served under a plain address may sit in a million browsers and thousands of edge caches, each keeping it as long as its headers allow. Sending a purge to every edge is slow and never quite complete, and a browser cannot be reached at all. And a half-updated map is worse than an old one: a new road drawn on one tile and missing from the tile beside it ends at the tile's edge.

The answer is to never change a tile at an address. Put a **version** of the whole map in every tile's address. A tile at a given version is fixed for ever, so it can be cached for ever.[^immutable] Each new version of the map is drawn alongside the old one, and when it is ready, the small file that tells pages the current version changes. That one file is served with a lifetime of a minute or so, while the tiles themselves are marked to be kept for a year. Pages then ask for the new addresses, and the old tiles, no longer asked for, age out of the caches by themselves.

blocks.caption: A versioned tile address. Nothing is ever purged: a new version means new addresses.

blocks.text: The price is a cold start: when the version changes, every edge cache misses on every tile at once, and the tile store takes a surge of requests until the caches fill again. That is a reason to change versions every few days rather than every edit, and to let edges fetch the new version's popular tiles before the switch. The same version number should cover the road data that lesson M3's route planner uses, so the map never shows a road the route planner does not know about.

A raster tile is a picture: the server has chosen every colour, every line width and every label, and the phone only shows it. Rotate the map and the labels turn upside down. Want a dark style at night, or labels in another language, and the server must draw and store the whole pyramid again.

In December 2010 Google Maps 5.0 for Android began drawing maps on the phone from **vector** data: the tiles carried the geometry of roads, coastlines and buildings, and the phone drew them, which let the map tilt into 3D and rotate with the labels upright. Mapbox published an open format for vector tiles in 2014, now widely used. Each tile holds the shapes that fall inside its square, clipped at the edges, with coordinates as whole numbers on a 4,096 by 4,096 grid, stored as small differences from the last point and packed in Protocol Buffers. The phone draws them with a style sheet it is sent once. Each tile also carries a margin of geometry a little past its edge, so a road crossing the edge is drawn the same on both sides, and the label placer avoids spots where a label would be cut.

Counting the cost, vector tiles move work from the server's disks to the phone's processor. They are usually several times smaller than the images of the same squares, one tile serves every style and language, and a tile can be drawn larger than its own zoom, so many vector maps stop cutting new tiles a few zooms short of the deepest raster zoom, which shrinks the pyramid by a factor of four for each zoom left out. Whole regions become small enough to download for use offline. In return every client needs a full drawing engine with fonts and label placement, old phones draw slowly, and the server no longer controls exactly what the reader sees.

blocks.caption: Map tiles on the web, from OpenStreetMap's start in 2004 to an open format for vector tiles in 2014.
Six questions on map tiles
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How many tiles are there at zoom 10 of a web map, where each zoom splits every tile into four?
items.why: Zoom 10 is 2^10 = 1,024 tiles across and 1,024 down, about 1.05 million in all.

items.ask: Why do tile services draw the low zooms ahead of time but the deepest zooms only when first requested?
choices: Deep-zoom tiles change too often to be worth storing, while low-zoom tiles hardly ever change
Deep-zoom tiles are drawn by the browser from low-zoom ones, so the server only stores the low ones
Low zooms are few and seen by everyone; deep zooms are vast in number and mostly never viewed
items.why: Each zoom has four times the tiles of the one above, and most deep tiles are sea, desert or farmland nobody looks at closely. Drawing on first view, then caching, spends effort only where people look.

items.ask: A map provider puts the map's version number in every tile's address. What does that buy?
choices: A tile never changes at its address, so caches keep it indefinitely and an update needs no purge
Old tiles are deleted from every browser and edge cache the moment a new version is published
Each tile can be updated on its own the moment an edit touches it, without waiting for others
items.why: New content gets new addresses, so nothing cached is ever wrong; old tiles stop being requested and expire. The page shows tiles from one version, so their edges match.

items.ask: What does a provider pay for switching every tile to a new version's address at once?
choices: Readers see tiles from two versions mixed on one screen until their browsers restart
Every cache misses on every tile at first, so the tile store takes a surge until caches refill
The tile store must keep both versions for ever, doubling its storage after each release
items.why: New addresses are cold everywhere. That is why versions change every few days rather than with each edit, and why popular tiles can be fetched ahead of the switch.

items.ask: What do vector tiles move from the server to the device?
choices: The map data itself: the device stores the whole world and asks the server for nothing
The tile cutting: the device splits one large image into squares as needed
The drawing: the device turns geometry into pixels with a style it holds
items.why: The server sends shapes, not pictures. One tile serves any style, language or rotation, at the cost of a drawing engine and processor time on every client.

items.ask: Storing every tile from zoom 0 to 18 at 20 KB each would take roughly how much?
items.why: Zooms 0 to 18 hold about 92 billion tiles, and 92 billion × 20 KB is about 1.8 PB if every tile is stored as its own image. Sharing one copy of the plain ocean square, as part 3 describes, removes most of that.

summary: **A web map is a pyramid of square tiles.** Zoom z has 4^z tiles of 256 pixels, each named by zoom, column and row.
**Each zoom multiplies the count by four.** Zoom 18, at about 60 cm a pixel, alone has about 69 billion tiles.
**Draw the few low zooms ahead, the vast deep ones on demand.** Most deep tiles are ocean or empty land that nobody looks at closely.
**Popularity is skewed, so caches carry the load.** Browser caches, edge caches and the tile store serve a tile drawn once to everyone after.
**Never change a tile at an address.** A map version in every tile's address lets every cache keep tiles for ever and makes updates need no purge.
**A version switch costs a cold start.** Every cache misses at once, so versions change every few days, not with every edit.
**Vector tiles send geometry instead of pictures.** The device draws them in any style or rotation, at the cost of a drawing engine on every client.

ajax.title: A name for the trick
ajax.text: Ten days after Google Maps opened, the designer Jesse James Garrett published an essay calling this way of building web pages Ajax: pages that fetch data in the background with JavaScript and update themselves without reloading. He cited Google Maps and Google Suggest as the examples.

mercator.title: Why 85 degrees
mercator.text: Mercator's projection stretches distances more and more toward the poles, and reaches them only at infinity. Cutting it at about 85.05° north and south makes the map exactly as tall as it is wide, a square that divides cleanly into tiles. The price is that the polar regions are missing and Greenland looks as large as Africa.

metatile.title: Metatiles
metatile.text: Drawing a map means loading every road, label and coastline in the area, and labels need room beyond the tile's edge. Drawing a block of 8 by 8 tiles as one image and cutting it up shares that work across 64 tiles, and keeps labels from being cut off at tile edges.

immutable.title: Caching for ever
immutable.text: An HTTP response can carry Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable, which tells every cache it may keep the file for a year and need never check it. That is safe only for an address whose content will never change, which is what the version in the address guarantees.
